e-12743.problem:
What is the negation of the following statement?

$$
\forall y \in \overline{S}, \, \neg P(y)
$$
e-12743.worked_solution:
To negate the universal statement $\forall y \in \overline{S}, \, \neg P(y),$ we flip the quantifier to existential and negate the predicate: 

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀y\in \overset{―}{S},\,¬P(y)) & ≡∃y\in \overset{―}{S},\,¬¬P(y) \\  & ≡∃y\in \overset{―}{S},\,P(y)\end{aligned}
$$

e-12744.problem:
Negate the following statement:

$\qquad$ For all $n \in \mathbb{N},$ $n$ is a composite number.
e-12744.worked_solution:
If we denote

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14108273/assets/b8d152c4a9f69b2a6ea0657d9e66ca4adbc11bc480d25a28ea07eac28a646ac3.png)

our statement can be written as

$$
\forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \, P(n).
$$

Negating this, we obtain

$$
\neg \left( \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \, P(n)  \right) \equiv \exists n \in \mathbb{N}, \, \neg P(n).
$$

Finally, $\exists n \in \mathbb{N}, \, \neg P(n)$ reads as follows:

$\qquad$ **There exists** $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $n$ is **not** a composite number.

e-12745.problem:
Negate the following statement: 

$\qquad$ Some quadrilaterals are squares.
e-12745.worked_solution:
Let $Q$ be the set of all quadrilaterals and $S$ the set of all squares. The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

$\qquad$ There exists $q \in Q$ such that $q \in S$

Introducing the existential quantifier, we get the following:

$\qquad$ $\exists q \in Q, \, q \in S.$

Negating this, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∃q\in Q,\,q\in S) & ≡∀q\in Q,\,¬(q\in S) \\  & ≡∀q\in Q,\,q\notin S\end{aligned}
$$

which reads 

$\qquad$ For all $q \in Q,$ $q \not\in S.$

or simply

$\qquad$ All quadrilaterals are not squares.

after.problem:
Negate the following statement:

$\,$ There exists $r\in Q$ such that ${r}^{2}=-1.$
after.worked_solution:
If we denote

$$
P(r):{r}^{2}=-1,
$$

our statement can be written as

$$
∃r\in Q,\,P(r).
$$

Negating this, we obtain

$$
¬(∃r\in Q,\,P(r))≡∀r\in Q,\,¬P(r).
$$

Finally, $∀r\in Q,\,¬P(r)$ reads as follows:

$\,$ **For all** $r\in Q,$ ${r}^{2}\ne -1.$

$\,$ There exists $n\in N$ such that $\frac{n}{10}\in N.$
after.worked_solution:
If we denote

$$
P(n):\frac{n}{10}\in N,
$$

our statement can be written as

$$
∃n\in N,\,P(n).
$$

Negating this, we obtain

$$
¬(∃n\in N,\,P(n))≡∀n\in N,\,¬P(n).
$$

Finally, $∀n\in N,\,¬P(n)$ reads as follows:

$\,$ **For all** $n\in N,$ $\frac{n}{10}\notin N.$
